Rill Fenlake.narrative: I was born on the lake's edge and I will die on it, in the old boathouse my father patched and I have patched twice since. I punt out before light with the mist on the water and I smoke what I catch in the shed behind the house; a good morning's catch keeps Gristle and me in meal and lamp oil. Nell Sedge lets me keep the boathouse for a share of the lake catch, and I pay it, though it is a lean share this year with the Coombes behind on their rent and no help coming. The Elmwick men trampled my nets when they came to pull Jem's fence down, and I have not sold a fish to anyone from Elmwick since, and I will not be talked round by soft words.
values: a fair share for a fair catch
my boathouse and my punt are mine
Elmwick folk came to fight, not to mend fences
smoke the fish clean and the buyer comes back
goals: keep the boathouse's standing with Nell Sedge paid up
get a new net made before the autumn run
see the Coombes through their thin rent without going short myself
keep Gristle off the deep water at the lake's middle
Rill Fenlake.mood: sore and stubborn, with a morning's work still to do

relations.name: Gristle Fenlake
relations.label: son
relations.note: He mends the punt better than I did at his age, and he is the whole of what I have.

relations.name: Morwen Coombe
relations.label: neighbour
relations.note: We trade cheese for smoked fish and neither of us has coin to spare; she worries the meadow will be taken and I know it might.

relations.name: Jem Coombe
relations.label: neighbour
relations.note: A decent man with a fence pulled down twice; I would help him mend it if I had the timber.

relations.name: Nell Sedge
relations.label: landlady
relations.note: She holds the boathouse's standing over me and I owe her a share of the catch; she has not squeezed me yet, but she could.

relations.name: Eadric Sedge
relations.label: friend
relations.note: He fishes the reeds and knows the water; we talk plain and he does not cheat on a trade.

relations.name: Thistle Mossfoot
relations.label: trade partner
relations.note: His packs take my smoked fish east and he brings back hooks and salt; a small folk pedlar keeps his word.

relations.name: Hob Garrow
relations.label: grudge
relations.note: His Elmwick men trampled my nets to dry and called it a fence quarrel; I will not sell him or his a fish.

relations.name: Tibbott Coombe
relations.label: neighbour
relations.note: Old Tibbott keeps the bees and the rent tally and remembers when the meadow was common; he is right and it does him no good.

memories.gist: The morning I found my drying nets trampled flat in the mud where the Elmwick men had walked over them pulling Jem's fence down; a whole morning's catch spoiled and one net torn past mending.
My father teaching me to pole the punt through the shallows by the reed beds, telling me the lake gives to those who read it and takes from those who don't.
The Lean Year, when the lake still gave fish but nobody had grain to trade for it, and I smoked everything and ate smoked fish till I could not stand the smell.
The night Gristle was born in the boathouse with only Morwen Coombe to help, and the punt knocking against the step in the wind all night.
Nell Sedge coming down to the boathouse to set the terms of my standing: a share of the lake catch each season, and no argument.
Gristle, six years old, poling the punt alone across the shallows and back while I watched from the shed with my heart in my mouth.

stances.why: They trampled my nets and spoiled a catch, and called it a fence quarrel.
The boathouse is my roof and my living; if I lose the standing I lose everything.
A clean smoke is what makes a buyer come back, and Thistle's packs carry my name east.
My father taught me the shallows and the pools, and they have never failed me entirely.
They are behind on their rent and I trade fish for cheese with them anyway; a neighbour who goes under is no good to anyone.

Rill Fenlake.secret: I have been holding back a little of Nell's share of the catch these last weeks, telling myself it is against a thin season, and I have not told her or anyone.

Gristle Fenlake.narrative: I live in the boathouse with Mam and help her with the punt and the smoke shed. I know where the shallow pools are and where the bottom drops away, and I do not go near the middle of the lake where it is deep and dark. I play with Osric Coombe when the goats bring him down to the meadow edge, and I can mend a net as well as anyone.
values: Mam knows best about the lake
the middle is deep and I stay out of it
a mended net is a good day's work
goals: learn to pole the punt all the way to the far reeds
catch a fish bigger than my arm
not think about the deep water

relations.name: Rill Fenlake
relations.label: mother
relations.note: She knows the lake better than anyone and she is cross with Elmwick, but not with me.

relations.name: Osric Coombe
relations.label: friend
relations.note: He plays at the meadow edge with the goats and we skip stones in the shallows.

relations.name: Morwen Coombe
relations.label: neighbour
relations.note: She brings cheese and milk and is kind to me.

relations.name: Tibbott Coombe
relations.label: neighbour
relations.note: Old Tibbott keeps the bees and tells me about when the meadow was common for everyone.

memories.gist: Poling the punt out to the shallows alone for the first time and Mam watching from the shed, and me not falling in.
The day the Elmwick men came and Mam shouted at them over her trampled nets, and I hid in the smoke shed till they had gone.

stances.why: The water goes dark and cold out there and I cannot see the bottom.
She works before light and I am the only one to help her.
